title: Mobil Oil Exploration & Producing Southeast, Inc. v. United States
lead: Offshore lessees bought a regulated opportunity to seek drilling permission, and a later statute substantially changed that promised process without guaranteeing that drilling ever would succeed.

actors.name: Mobil and Marathon
actors.role: Oil companies seeking return of offshore lease bonuses

actors.name: United States
actors.role: Lessor acting through Interior and Commerce

actors.name: North Carolina
actors.role: Coastal state objecting to consistency of exploration

actors.name: Environmental Sciences Review Panel
actors.role: New review body required by later legislation

proceedings: Court of Federal Claims: summary judgment finding repudiation and awarding bonus restitution.
Federal Circuit: reversed based on North Carolina’s independent objection.
Supreme Court: reversed and remanded 8–1 for proceedings consistent with restitution.
limits: No right to drill, profitable production, invalidation of environmental legislation, or resolution of every expense claim followed. The unchallenged rejection of sovereign-acts defense was not reconsidered.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The companies buy an opportunity governed by specified procedures
sections.cue: Introduce the leases and the multiple remaining approvals.
paragraphs: In 1981, Mobil and Marathon paid about $156 million in bonuses for ten-year renewable federal leases off North Carolina. Annual rent and future production royalties were additional obligations. The leases did not guarantee drilling or profit. They supplied an opportunity to seek approvals under incorporated laws and regulations, including the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and Coastal Zone Management Act.

Interior had to consider an Exploration Plan and approve a qualifying plan within thirty days. Drilling also required coastal-zone consistency certification, subject to state objection and possible Commerce override. Discharge permits and a later development-and-production plan required further approvals. Passing the first stage did not complete the project.

In 1989, the companies, North Carolina, and Interior agreed on draft-plan review and an environmental report. Interior would suspend about $250,000 annual rent and extend leases while specified preparatory and state-objection matters remained. Following extensive review, the companies submitted a final plan and consistency certification August 20, 1990. Congress’s Outer Banks Protection Act had taken effect two days earlier.

sections.title: The new statute prevents approval under the old process
sections.cue: Trace agency action and the contract litigation.
paragraphs: The new law barred plans and drilling permits for at least thirteen months. It required an Environmental Sciences Review Panel report, Interior certification to Congress, and another congressional-session period, with explanations for departures from panel recommendations. Interior told Mobil the plan satisfied existing requirements and could not properly be disapproved under them, but the new law blocked approval. It held the plan and suspended the leases.

After the report, Interior certified sufficient information yet awaited recommended studies. North Carolina objected in November 1990. The companies sought Commerce override, denied in 1994 substantially on panel findings. Congress repealed the new statute in 1996.

The companies joined a Court of Federal Claims action in October 1992. On summary judgment, that court found repudiation and awarded return of the bonuses. A divided Federal Circuit reversed because the state objection independently prevented exploration. The Supreme Court reviewed both companies’ cases together.

sections.title: The majority finds a substantial change to the purchased opportunity
sections.cue: Explain the contractual standard and incorporated-law defenses.
paragraphs: Justice Breyer wrote for eight Justices. Ordinary government-contract principles allowed restitution after repudiation or nonperformance amounting to total breach, requiring substantial impairment rather than any minor delay. Once justified, restitution could restore an advance even if eventual performance would have been financially disadvantageous. The opinion’s overvalued-land and lottery illustrations distinguished receiving the purchased opportunity from obtaining a profitable outcome.

The incorporated-law defenses failed. A statutory suspension provision required a lessee request not established for this delay. Existing environmental-review regulations did not incorporate every analysis demanded by unknown future statutes. Although the leases expressly incorporated some future regulations under named laws, their catchall did not make the process infinitely changeable through later legislation. Serious-environmental-harm authority likewise did not justify this delay when Interior had said existing standards were met. Its actually cited judicial-decree regulation was inapplicable because no decree existed, as the Government conceded.

The new law changed not just timing but later permits, review institutions, and treatment of panel recommendations. The United States was the contracting obligor; announcing adherence to inconsistent legislation communicated departure from the bargain. The majority rejected the view that generally directed legislation could never communicate repudiation. It did not reconsider sovereign acts, because the Government did not challenge the trial court’s rejection of that defense.

sections.title: Neither continued requests nor the state objection defeat restitution
sections.cue: Distinguish substantial breach, waiver, and compensatory loss.
paragraphs: Timely, fair processing was a gateway through several discretionary approvals, not an incidental thirty-day detail. The announced minimum thirteen-month delay ultimately lasted at least four years and substantially narrowed that gateway. Interior approval also could matter in seeking Commerce action. The majority therefore found substantial deprivation and repudiation.

Urging performance did not itself waive restitution. Nor did the Government show significant accepted postrepudiation performance. Submitting a plan showed what the companies requested, not what they received. Commerce substantially relied on the new panel rather than supplying the original promised process. Lease suspensions were independently due under the 1989 memorandum, and the Government did not establish significant performance of the repudiated leases. No retraction was claimed.

The state objection and uncertainty of all permits might matter to compensatory damages for lost performance, but these companies sought restoration of advances after repudiation. They need not prove certain permission or profit to recover the price of an opportunity the Government had substantially altered.

sections.title: Stevens would limit relief to the consequences of delay
sections.cue: Preserve the dissent and precise remand.
paragraphs: Justice Stevens agreed that withholding qualifying-plan approval beyond thirty days breached the leases but disputed repudiation, materiality, and the full refund. He stressed known state opposition, federal environmental work, continued pursuit of approvals, and efforts to preserve the project. Interior considered the plan; its fault was withholding approval, not unfair consideration.

For him, legislation addressed the public or Secretary rather than communicated contractual abandonment. Letters announced suspension, not cancellation, and continued performance and requested suspensions contradicted repudiation. He distinguished an external legal restriction from changing contract terms. Materiality had to be judged at breach across the whole venture. North Carolina objected sixty days after the approval deadline and, absent override, independently barred drilling. One approval letter was only one gateway, its supposed effect on Commerce disputed, with evidence the new statute did not impede override review. Stevens favored at most modest delay damages, regarding $156 million as disproportionate relief from known investment risk.

On June 26, 2000, the Court reversed and remanded both cases for proceedings consistent with restitution of the bonuses. It neither ordered drilling nor invalidated the environmental policy. The result protected the contracted process despite uncertainty of eventual permission.
